title: How to Help an Anxious Child
excerpt: An anxious child does not need their fear erased or argued away. They need a steady adult to borrow calm from until they grow their own.
body:
When your child is anxious, every instinct in you wants to fix it, fast. You want to reassure the fear out of existence, to prove with logic that the monster is not real, to make the bad feeling stop because watching it is unbearable. Almost none of that works, and some of it makes things worse. An anxious child is not asking you to solve the problem. They are asking whether they are safe, and whether you can hold what they cannot.

This is gentle work, and it is slow. There is no sentence that ends anxiety. But there are ways of being with a frightened child that, over time, teach their nervous system that the world is more bearable than it feels.

## Do not argue with the fear

The reflex is to reason. "There is nothing to be scared of. That could never happen. You are being silly." To the anxious child, this lands as: you do not understand, and now I am also wrong for feeling this. Anxiety does not respond to argument because it does not come from the reasoning part of the mind. You cannot debate it into submission.

Instead, name it and stay near it. "That feels really scary right now. I am right here." You are not agreeing that the danger is real. You are agreeing that the fear is real, which it is, and a child whose fear is acknowledged settles faster than one whose fear is dismissed.

## Be the calm they borrow

Children regulate their emotions by borrowing yours first. A small child who falls looks at the parent's face to decide how hurt to be. The anxious child does the same with fear. If you meet their panic with panic, you have doubled it. If you meet it with steadiness, you have handed them something solid to hold.

This is hard, because an anxious child often has an anxious parent, and the fear in the room is partly yours. Do your own breathing first. Lower your voice. Slow your body down. You are not faking calm; you are choosing to go first into it, so they have a path to follow. "Cast all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you," Peter writes. Part of how a child learns to cast their fear on God is by first casting it on a parent who does not flinch.

## Teach the body, not just the mind

Anxiety lives in the body, so help the body before you talk to the mind. Slow breathing, in through the nose, out long and slow, with you doing it alongside them. A hand on the chest to feel it settle. Naming five things they can see in the room. These are not tricks. They are ways of telling an alarmed nervous system that it is safe to stand down.

Do this when they are calm, too, not only mid-panic. A child who has practiced these in peace can reach for them in the storm. You are giving them tools they will carry into adulthood, long after they stop needing your hand.

## Hand the fear to God, honestly

The Christian answer to fear is not that fear is faithless and must be hidden. The Psalms are full of frightened people speaking their fear plainly to God. Teach your child to do the same. Pray with them, out loud, naming the actual fear. "God, the dark feels scary tonight. Please be near. Help us not be afraid."

Do not promise them that nothing bad will ever happen, because that is not a promise God makes and your child will eventually catch you in it. Promise them instead that they are not alone in it, that God is near the brokenhearted, and that you are not going anywhere. That is a promise you can keep.

## This week

The next time your child is anxious, resist the urge to argue the fear away. Name it, get your own body calm first, and breathe slowly alongside them until the wave passes. Then, on an ordinary calm evening, pray with them and let them speak their real fear out loud to God. You are teaching them, one settled moment at a time, that fear can be carried and that they do not have to carry it alone. If the anxiety is constant or growing, do not white-knuckle it; a wise counselor is a gift, not a failure.
